scenarios.title: Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.brief: A meal-kit company runs a customer support agent on the Claude Agent SDK. Its MCP tools are get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human and pause_subscription. The agent may refund up to $150 per box; larger refunds go to a human.

questions.question: The agent's loop ends the turn whenever Claude's response contains a text block. Claude often writes a short line, such as “Let me check that box,” in the same response where it asks to call lookup_order. In those chats the lookup never runs. The customer waits for an answer that never comes. Which change to the loop fixes this?

options.t: Tell Claude in the system prompt not to write any text in a response that calls a tool.
options.why: Works, but only usually. Claude would write fewer of those lines, but the loop still ends on text, so any line that slips through stops the lookup again.

options.t: Set tool_choice to any on the first request after each customer message.
options.why: Works, but wrong lever. A forced tool call carries no text, so this case stops, but Claude must now call a tool even when it should just answer.

options.t: Branch on stop_reason: run the tools and loop on tool_use, stop on end_turn.
options.why: Best. A response can hold text and a tool request together. stop_reason says what comes next: tool_use means run the tools and continue, end_turn means the turn is over.

options.t: When a turn ends without an answer, send Claude a short “please continue” message.
options.why: Works, but hides the problem. The nudge restarts the stalled chat, but the loop still ends early, and every stall costs an extra request.

questions.decider: The agent's loop ends the turn whenever Claude's response contains a text block.
questions.explanation: The loop should be driven by stop_reason: continue on tool_use, stop on end_turn. Checking for text in the response is an anti-pattern, because text and tool calls can arrive together.

eli5.question: Claude says “Let me check that box” and asks for a lookup in the same breath. The loop hears the words and hangs up before the lookup runs. The clue: the loop decides by looking for text.
eli5.answer: Imagine a waiter who walks away as soon as you start talking, even when you were in the middle of ordering. The fix is to wait for a clear signal: “that's all”. Each Claude response carries that signal, called stop_reason. Rule: tool_use → run the tool and keep going. end_turn → stop.
options: Asking Claude to stay quiet helps, but the waiter still walks off at the first word.
Forcing a tool call stops the chatter, but now Claude must call a tool even when it should just reply.
Correct. Listen for the real “that's all” signal.
Calling the waiter back each time works, but he keeps walking off.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think Claude talks too much and should be told to be quiet. But the text is harmless. The bug is in the loop: it treats any text as the end of the turn. The API already says whether the turn is over, in stop_reason.
deep.diagram:
response = text + tool_use
  stop_reason = tool_use → run tool, send result, loop
  stop_reason = end_turn → turn over, reply to customer
deep.mapTitle: What should end an agent's turn?

head: Signal
Use it to stop?
Why
rows: The API's own signal that Claude is done
Text and tool calls can come together
It cuts off work that is not finished

evidence.quote: The agent's loop ends the turn whenever Claude's response contains a text block
evidence.means: The decider. The stop rule looks at content, not at the signal. A prompt rule ([[0]]) and a nudge ([[3]]) leave that rule in place.

evidence.quote: Claude often writes a short line, such as “Let me check that box,” in the same response where it asks to call lookup_order
evidence.means: Text and a tool request arrive together. That is normal, so the loop must handle it.

evidence.quote: In those chats the lookup never runs
evidence.means: Claude did ask for the tool. Forcing tool calls ([[1]]) answers a different problem: Claude not asking.

evidence.quote: Which change to the loop fixes this?
evidence.means: Change the stop rule to stop_reason: [[2]].

deep.rule: Loop on stop_reason: tool_use → run tools and continue; end_turn → stop. Never stop because text appeared.

guide.quote: Continue the loop when stop_reason == "tool_use"; terminate when "end_turn".

questions.question: The coordinator sends refund eligibility questions to a policy subagent with the Task tool. The prompt it sends reads: “Check whether this customer's claim is eligible.” The subagent's verdicts are vague and often hedge. The facts it needs came up earlier in the chat: which items spoiled, when the box arrived, and what the customer wants. Which change best improves the verdicts?

options.t: Spell out the spoiled items, the arrival day and the remedy wanted in each Task call.
options.why: Best. A subagent does not see the coordinator's chat. Whatever it needs must be written into the prompt it receives, and the coordinator already has these facts.

options.t: Give the policy subagent read-only get_customer and lookup_order tools.
options.why: Works, but only in part. The tools would return the order and its arrival day, but which items spoiled and what the customer wants exist only in the chat.

options.t: Add the refund policy and two worked verdicts to the policy subagent's system prompt.
options.why: Works, but different problem. Policy text and examples improve how the subagent reasons, but it still does not know this customer's case.

options.t: Forward the whole chat transcript to the policy subagent with each Task call.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. The facts would be in there, but buried among greetings and side talk. A short, chosen summary of the case is cheaper and clearer.

questions.decider: The facts it needs came up earlier in the chat
questions.explanation: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation. The coordinator must pass the facts the subagent needs, explicitly and in a focused form, in the Task prompt.

eli5.question: A manager asks a specialist “Is this claim OK?” without saying what the claim is. The clue: the facts are only in the manager's head (the chat).
eli5.answer: A specialist you phone has not heard your earlier conversation with the customer. You have to tell them: “two salmon packs spoiled, box came Tuesday, customer wants a refund.” A subagent is that specialist, and the Task prompt is the phone call. Rule: a subagent knows only what you put in its prompt.
options: Correct. Tell the specialist the facts of the case.
Letting the specialist look things up finds the order, but not what the customer said.
A better rulebook helps the specialist judge, but they still don't know the case.
Forwarding the whole call recording works, but they must dig through it to find the facts.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the subagent knows what the coordinator knows. It does not. Each subagent starts with only its own system prompt and the prompt it is sent. Facts that came up in the chat reach it only if the coordinator writes them in.
deep.diagram:
chat: spoiled salmon, Tuesday, wants refund
  coordinator ─ Task prompt ─→ policy subagent
  (facts must be IN the prompt; nothing is inherited)
deep.mapTitle: A subagent gives weak answers. What is missing?

head: What you observe
Cause
Fix
rows: Vague, hedged verdicts; facts were in the chat
Write the facts into the Task prompt
Facts are present but the reasoning is off
Policy text and examples in its system prompt
Prompt is huge and the answer misses key points
Pass a focused summary of the case

evidence.quote: The prompt it sends reads: “Check whether this customer's claim is eligible.”
evidence.means: The prompt names no facts. The subagent has nothing to judge.

evidence.quote: The subagent's verdicts are vague and often hedge
evidence.means: That is what a reasoner does with no facts. Better policy text ([[2]]) doesn't add any.

evidence.quote: The facts it needs came up earlier in the chat
evidence.means: The decider. Only the coordinator has them, so tools ([[1]]) can't fetch the customer's words.

evidence.quote: Which change best improves the verdicts?
evidence.means: Pass the chosen facts, not the whole transcript ([[3]]): [[0]].

deep.rule: Subagents inherit nothing. Put the facts they need into the Task prompt, in a focused form.

guide.obj: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
guide.quote: Subagent context must be provided explicitly in the prompt (no automatic inheritance / shared memory).

questions.question: Customers who want to cancel are handed to a person through escalate_to_human. Product would like the agent to suggest pausing the subscription first, before it hands the customer over. This is a retention idea, not a business rule, so the agent does not have to do it in every chat. What is the most appropriate way to add it?

options.t: Add a system-prompt instruction to suggest a pause, plus two short example chats.
options.why: Best. A soft behaviour, where an occasional miss does no harm, is what prompt guidance is for. One instruction and two examples are easy to maintain.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks escalate_to_human until a pause has been offered.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. The hook would make the offer happen every time, but it needs code to spot cancellations and track what was said. Guarantees are for business rules.

options.t: Add the pause offer to the escalate_to_human description, so Claude offers it before calling the tool.
options.why: Works, but wrong home. Claude does read tool descriptions, but they explain when and how to call a tool. How to talk to the customer belongs in the system prompt, where it is easy to find and change.

options.t: Route every cancellation request to a new retention subagent before it reaches a human.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. A retention subagent could make the offer well, but it adds a handoff and another prompt to maintain, for one sentence of behaviour.

questions.decider: This is a retention idea, not a business rule, so the agent does not have to do it in every chat.
questions.explanation: Programmatic enforcement is for steps that must happen every time. A best-effort suggestion is shaped with a clear instruction plus a few examples.

eli5.question: Product wants the agent to ask “would you like to pause instead?” before it hands a cancellation to a person. The clue: it's a retention idea, not a business rule.
eli5.answer: A shop asks staff to mention the loyalty card at the till. A note and a quick demo do the job; nobody installs a till that locks until the card is mentioned. Here the note is a system-prompt instruction and the demo is example chats. Rule: must happen every time → code. Nice to have → prompt and examples.
options: Correct. A plain instruction plus examples sets the nudge.
A lock in code (a hook) is for things that must never be skipped. Here skipping is allowed.
Tool instructions would work, but they're the wrong place for how to talk to customers.
A whole new helper agent for one friendly sentence is too much.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the most reliable option is always the best one. The question asks for the most appropriate one. Code-level enforcement (a hook) is right when a step must happen every time, such as checking identity before a refund. For a nice-to-have it is extra machinery: something has to detect cancellations and remember what was said.
deep.diagram:
Must it happen every time?
  yes → hook or prerequisite gate (code)
  no  → prompt instruction + examples
deep.mapTitle: How firmly must this behaviour hold?

head: Situation
Right mechanism
Why
rows: A suggestion or tone; an occasional miss is harmless
A business rule; a miss costs money or breaks policy
Hook or prerequisite gate in code
Prompts have a non-zero failure rate
Sensitive data must never reach the model
The model can't repeat what it never saw
Guidance on when and how to call a tool
Claude reads it when choosing tools
Instructions are clear but output still varies

evidence.quote: Product would like the agent to suggest pausing the subscription first, before it hands the customer over
evidence.means: The goal is a suggestion in the conversation. That belongs in Claude's instructions, not in a tool's description ([[2]]).

evidence.quote: This is a retention idea, not a business rule, so the agent does not have to do it in every chat
evidence.means: The decider. Missing it now and then is harmless, so a hook ([[1]]) or a new subagent ([[3]]) is more than the goal needs.

evidence.quote: What is the most appropriate way to add it?
evidence.means: “Most appropriate” means the right size: an instruction with examples, [[0]].

deep.rule: Business rule → enforce it in code. Suggestion or style → prompt instruction plus examples.

guide.obj: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
guide.quote: Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) vs prompt-based guidance.

questions.question: get_customer returns the full card number on file, and the team that owns that server will not change it. Twice, the agent read a card number to a customer. Security says this must never happen. What is the best fix?

options.t: Add a system-prompt rule to mention cards by their last four digits only, with two examples.
options.why: Works, but only usually. A clear rule with examples cuts the leaks, but prompts have a non-zero failure rate, and this is a must-never.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that masks the card field in results before Claude reads them.
options.why: Best. The hook changes the result before Claude reads it, so the agent can't repeat a number it never saw. The server stays as it is.

options.t: Route get_customer through a subagent told to pass on only the name, plan and box IDs.
options.why: Works, but still a model choosing. The subagent sees the full number and decides what to pass on; its instructions are not a filter.

options.t: Scan each reply for card-number patterns and block the reply before it reaches the customer.
options.why: Works, but only for the formats it knows. A number read out with spaces or in parts slips past, and Claude still has the number.

questions.decider: Security says this must never happen.
questions.explanation: When a tool returns data the model must never use, change the result with a PostToolUse hook before the model sees it. Prompt rules only make misuse less likely.

eli5.question: The agent sometimes reads a customer's card number out loud. The clue: security says this must never happen.
eli5.answer: If a receptionist must never read out card numbers, don't hand them the number: black it out on the paper first. A PostToolUse hook is that black marker. It edits each tool result before Claude reads it, and Claude can't repeat what it never saw. Rule: if the model must never use some data, remove it before the model sees it.
options: A written rule usually works, but “usually” isn't enough for a must-never.
Correct. Black out the number before Claude ever sees it.
A helper told to pass on only some fields still sees the number, and might pass it on.
Checking each reply catches the obvious cases, but Claude still knows the number.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a firm instruction stops the model saying something. It lowers the chance, but prompt compliance is probabilistic. For data that must never reach a customer, the reliable place to act is the tool result itself: change it before the model reads it.
deep.diagram:
get_customer → [PostToolUse: mask card] → Claude
server unchanged        model never sees the number

head: Need
Mechanism
Where it acts
rows: Model must never see or repeat a field
On the result, before Claude reads it
An action must never run in some case
On the call, before the tool runs
You own the tool and nobody needs the field

evidence.quote: get_customer returns the full card number on file, and the team that owns that server will not change it
evidence.means: The fix has to happen on the agent's side, between the tool and Claude.

evidence.quote: Twice, the agent read a card number to a customer
evidence.means: The number reaches Claude in ordinary chats. Scanning replies ([[3]]) catches only the patterns it knows.

evidence.quote: Security says this must never happen
evidence.means: The decider: a must-never. A prompt rule ([[0]]) and a subagent told what to pass on ([[2]]) both still rely on the model choosing.

evidence.quote: What is the best fix?
evidence.means: Change the result before Claude sees it: [[1]].

deep.rule: Model must never use some data? Strip it from the tool result with a PostToolUse hook.

guide.obj: 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
guide.quote: PostToolUse hooks intercept results for transformation before the model sees them.

questions.question: After each chat, a wrap-up request asks Claude to log the outcome. It should call one of three tools: record_resolved, record_escalated or record_abandoned. When Claude calls one, it picks the right tool. But sometimes it replies with a text summary instead, and that chat is never logged. Which change fits best?

options.t: Ask Claude for the outcome first, then force that record tool by name in tool_choice.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. Forcing by name does make the call happen, but it needs an extra request per chat and code to read the outcome first.

options.t: Add a line to the wrap-up prompt saying a record tool must be called every time.
options.why: Works, but only usually. A firm line reduces text replies, but with tool_choice on auto Claude can still answer in text.

options.t: Check stop_reason on the wrap-up reply and resend it with a reminder if it is end_turn.
options.why: Works, but too late. Catching the miss and resending gets the chat logged, but it costs extra calls when the API can require a tool call up front.

options.t: Set tool_choice to any for that final wrap-up step, and leave auto elsewhere.
options.why: Best. any requires a tool call but still lets Claude choose which one, and its choices are already right.

questions.decider: When Claude calls one, it picks the right tool.
questions.explanation: tool_choice any guarantees a tool call while leaving the choice of tool to Claude. Use it when a call must happen and selection already works.

eli5.question: At the end of each chat Claude should fill in one of three forms. It picks the right form, but sometimes writes a note instead. The clue: the choice is fine; the problem is skipping the form.
eli5.answer: Think of a clerk who must stamp one of three boxes before leaving. You don't tell them which box; you just say “you can't leave without stamping one.” In the API that rule is tool_choice: any. Rule: must call some tool, Claude picks which → any. Must call one specific tool → force it by name.
options: Asking first, then forcing the box, works but takes two trips.
A sign saying “please stamp” usually works, not every time.
Checking after and sending them back works, but costs a second trip.
Correct. Make stamping a box required, and let the clerk pick which.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a firmer instruction will stop the text replies. But with tool_choice on auto, a text reply is always allowed. The API has a setting that requires a tool call while still letting Claude choose the tool.
deep.diagram:
auto → Claude may reply in text (logs missed)
any  → must call a tool, Claude picks which one
tool → must call this one named tool

head: Need
Setting
Effect
rows: Some tool must be called; Claude chooses

evidence.quote: When Claude calls one, it picks the right tool
evidence.means: The decider. Selection works, so Claude should keep choosing. Forcing one tool by name ([[0]]) needs an extra step to pick it.

evidence.quote: But sometimes it replies with a text summary instead, and that chat is never logged
evidence.means: The call must happen every time. A prompt line ([[1]]) only makes it more likely.

evidence.quote: Which change fits best?
evidence.means: Prevent the miss rather than catch it ([[2]]): [[3]].

deep.rule: A tool call must happen and Claude picks the right tool? Set tool_choice to any.

guide.obj: 2.3 Distribute tools across agents and configure tool choice
guide.quote: "any" guarantees a tool call rather than text

questions.question: Customers usually describe a box by when it arrived, for example “last Tuesday's box”. The agent passes that date to lookup_order as the box ID, and the call fails. Each customer's box IDs are listed in their get_customer record. The description of lookup_order is one line: “Looks up a box.” What is the most effective first step?

options.t: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt that turn a delivery date into a box ID first.
options.why: Works, but leaves the cause in place. Examples would teach the date-to-ID step, but they add tokens to every request while the one-line description stays unclear. They are a later step.

options.t: Add a routing layer that detects dates and calls get_customer before lookup_order.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt for a first step. Code that spots dates and calls get_customer first would fix this case, but it is fragile and far more work than a better description.

options.t: Expand the lookup_order description with the ID format, an example, and where IDs come from.
options.why: Best. Claude learns how to call a tool mainly from its description. This one gives no ID format and no route from a date to an ID, and fixing that is cheap.

options.t: Add a lookup_order_by_date tool that takes a delivery date and returns the box.
options.why: Works, but more than a first step. A date-based tool would handle this request, but it is new code, and with equally thin descriptions the agent can misuse it too.

questions.decider: The description of lookup_order is one line: “Looks up a box.”
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the main signal for how to call a tool. A minimal description should first be expanded with input format, examples, edge cases and boundaries.

eli5.question: The agent keeps putting a date where a box ID should go. The clue: the tool's instructions are four words long.
eli5.answer: If a form field just says “Box”, people write all sorts of things in it. Write “Box ID, like BX-20431, found on the customer record” and most mistakes stop. For Claude, the tool description is that label. Rule: tool misused and its description is thin → fix the description first.
options: Examples help later, but the label itself is still unclear.
A program that hunts for dates in messages is a lot of work for a first step.
Correct. Fix the label: say what an ID looks like and where to find it.
A second tool with an equally vague label can go wrong the same way.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the agent needs more examples or smarter routing. But Claude decides how to call a tool mainly from the tool's description. “Looks up a box” gives no ID format and no hint that IDs come from get_customer. Fix that first: it is cheap and it fixes the cause.
deep.diagram:
"Looks up a box" → Claude guesses → date as ID → fail
+ ID format, example, where IDs come from → right call
deep.mapTitle: A tool is called wrongly. What do you fix first?

head: What you observe
Where the fault is
First fix
rows: Wrong input passed; the description is one line
Two similar tools get mixed up
Descriptions are detailed; behaviour still varies
Agent prefers Grep over a better MCP tool

evidence.quote: Customers usually describe a box by when it arrived
evidence.means: The agent gets a date, so the tool must explain how to get from a date to an ID.

evidence.quote: The agent passes that date to lookup_order as the box ID, and the call fails
evidence.means: The agent doesn't know what a box ID looks like. That is a description problem, not a routing problem ([[1]]).

evidence.quote: Each customer's box IDs are listed in their get_customer record
evidence.means: The data to fix it already exists. The agent just isn't told where to look, which a description can say.

evidence.quote: The description of lookup_order is one line: “Looks up a box.”
evidence.means: The decider. The cause is a thin description, so examples ([[0]]) and a new tool ([[3]]) work around it.

evidence.quote: What is the most effective first step?
evidence.means: First step = the cheapest change that fixes the cause: [[2]].

deep.rule: A tool gets the wrong input and its description is thin? Expand the description first.

guide.obj: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
guide.quote: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for selection

questions.question: pause_subscription fails when the next box is already past its packing cut-off. The cut-off depends on the delivery region, and only the backend knows it. Today the tool returns isError with the text “Request failed.” The agent retries several times, then tells the customer the system is down. Which change is best?

options.t: Add a check_pause_window tool that the agent calls before every pause attempt.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. A new tool would show the cut-off in advance, but it is new code and an extra call, while the real fault is an error that says nothing.

options.t: Return a business error with isRetryable false, the cut-off and next pausable box.
options.why: Best. The failure is a policy outcome, not an outage. A business category with isRetryable false stops the retries, and the details give the agent something true to tell the customer.

options.t: Return isError with the text “Too late to pause this box. Try the next one.”
options.why: Works, but only usually. A clear message helps the agent explain, but without a category or retry flag it must guess whether retrying could help.

options.t: Add a hook that blocks a second pause_subscription call and tells the agent to escalate.
options.why: Works, but wrong action. The retries stop, but a human gets a case the agent could have explained itself, and still with no reason.

questions.decider: Today the tool returns isError with the text “Request failed.”
questions.explanation: MCP tools should return structured errors: a category (transient, validation, business, permission), whether a retry can help, and a human-readable explanation. Business-rule failures are not retryable.

eli5.question: The pause tool fails because it's too late for this box, but it only says “Request failed.” So the agent keeps retrying and then blames an outage. The clue: the error message tells the agent nothing.
eli5.answer: If a shop till just beeps “error”, the cashier tries again and again. If it says “Sale item: no returns”, the cashier stops and explains. A structured error is that clear message: what kind of failure, whether trying again can help, and what to tell the customer. Rule: a business-rule failure → category business, not retryable, plus a plain reason.
options: A “check first” button helps, but it's a new button to build while the till still beeps “error”.
Correct. Say what kind of failure it is, that retrying won't help, and what to offer instead.
A clearer message helps, but the agent still has to guess whether to try again.
Stopping the retries works, but the case goes to a person who didn't need to see it.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the agent should know the rule in advance. But the cut-off depends on the region and only the backend knows it. The backend already knows why the call failed. The fix is to let the error say so, in a form the agent can act on.
deep.diagram:
now:   "Request failed" → retry, retry → "system down"
fixed: business, isRetryable=false, cut-off, next box
       → "Too late for this box; I can pause the next"
deep.mapTitle: What should a tool error tell the agent?

evidence.quote: The cut-off depends on the delivery region, and only the backend knows it
evidence.means: The backend has the answer. Its error should carry it, instead of a new lookup tool ([[0]]).

evidence.quote: Today the tool returns isError with the text “Request failed.”
evidence.means: The decider: the error carries no category, no retry hint and no reason. Better text alone ([[2]]) still leaves the retry question open.

evidence.quote: The agent retries several times, then tells the customer the system is down
evidence.means: The agent treats a policy outcome as an outage. Blocking retries ([[3]]) stops the loop but sends the case to a person.

evidence.quote: Which change is best?
evidence.means: A structured business error with a reason and an alternative: [[1]].

deep.rule: Business-rule failure? Return a structured error: category business, not retryable, with a reason the agent can tell the customer.

guide.obj: 2.2 Implement structured error responses for MCP tools
guide.quote: retriable: false + customer-friendly explanation for business violations

questions.question: A customer writes: “My salmon was missing again. I want to speak to a real person.” The refund is well inside the agent's limit, so the agent could settle the case alone. The customer sounds calm, and the request for a person is clear. How should the agent respond?

options.t: Say sorry, offer the refund it can issue now, and escalate if the customer asks for a person again.
options.why: Works, but wrong action. Many customers would take the refund, but this one asked for a person and now has to ask twice.

options.t: Run lookup_order to confirm the missing salmon, then escalate with what it found.
options.why: Works, but delays the request. The check adds a detail to the handoff, but the customer waits for a decision that is already made.

options.t: Call escalate_to_human at once, with a note that the customer asked for a person.
options.why: Works, but thin handoff. The customer reaches a person quickly, but the person must ask again which box and item it was about.

options.t: Call escalate_to_human at once, passing the customer ID, the box and the missing item.
options.why: Best. An explicit request for a person is a reason to escalate on its own. Passing the facts lets the person pick up without asking again.

questions.decider: I want to speak to a real person.
questions.explanation: When a customer explicitly asks for a human, escalate immediately, even if the agent could resolve the case. Hand over the key facts in a structured way so the human does not need to re-ask.

eli5.question: A customer says “I want a real person.” The agent could fix the problem itself. The clue: the customer asked directly.
eli5.answer: If you ask a shop assistant for the manager, you don't want to hear “but I can help you!” first. A good assistant fetches the manager and says “this customer's salmon was missing from box 3.” That's escalate at once, with a handoff that has the facts. Rule: explicit request for a human → escalate now, and pass the case details.
options: Offering a fix first is kind, but the customer already said what they want.
Checking the order first makes them wait for something they didn't ask for.
Fetching the manager is right, but the manager has to ask everything again.
Correct. Fetch the manager now and tell them what happened.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the agent should resolve what it can, because the refund is within its limit. That is right when a customer is unhappy but hasn't asked for a person. An explicit request for a human is its own trigger: honour it straight away.
deep.diagram:
"I want a real person" → escalate now
  handoff: customer ID, box, missing item
  person picks up without asking again
deep.mapTitle: When should the agent hand over to a person?

head: Situation
Agent's move
Why
rows: Customer explicitly asks for a person
Escalate at once, with the facts
Frustrated, simple case, no request for a person
Offer the fix it can make
A gap needs a human call

evidence.quote: I want to speak to a real person
evidence.means: The decider: an explicit request. Offering a refund first ([[0]]) makes the customer ask twice.

evidence.quote: The refund is well inside the agent's limit, so the agent could settle the case alone
evidence.means: Being able to resolve it is not a reason to override the request, or to stop for a lookup ([[1]]).

evidence.quote: How should the agent respond?
evidence.means: Escalate now, with the facts so the person doesn't re-ask (unlike [[2]]): [[3]].

deep.rule: Customer asks for a human? Escalate immediately and pass the case facts in the handoff.

guide.quote: Escalate immediately on explicit demand; offer resolution when straightforward.

questions.obj: 5.3 Access failure vs valid empty result
questions.question: The policy subagent checks a customer's past refunds through a payments API. When that API times out, the subagent tells the coordinator “No previous refunds found.” The coordinator then approves refunds that repeat earlier ones. The API's outages usually last about an hour. How should the subagent report this case?

options.t: As a failed lookup, naming the query it tried and any past refunds it did get back.
options.why: Best. A failed lookup must look different from a real empty result. With the failure, the query and any partial results, the coordinator can hold the refund, escalate or try later.

options.t: Retry with backoff first, then report “history unavailable” if every retry fails.
options.why: Works, but delays the problem. Retries help with short blips, but hour-long outages outlast them, and a bare status drops what was tried and found.

options.t: As an error marked “transient”, so the coordinator reruns the subagent later.
options.why: Works, but loses detail. It separates failure from empty, which is half the fix, but drops the query and any partial results the coordinator could use now.

options.t: As before, but the coordinator escalates every refund where no past refunds come back.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. No repeat refunds slip through, but every genuine first-time claim goes to a person too, and the timeout still looks like “none”.

questions.decider: When that API times out, the subagent tells the coordinator “No previous refunds found.”
questions.explanation: Subagents must distinguish access failures from valid empty results, and report failures with context: what was attempted, the error type and any partial results, so the coordinator can decide what to do.

eli5.question: The refund-history check sometimes can't reach the payments system, and then reports “no past refunds.” So the boss approves repeat refunds. The clue: “couldn't check” is reported as “nothing there.”
eli5.answer: If you can't open a filing cabinet, you don't tell your boss “the folder is empty.” You say “the cabinet was locked; I looked for Jo's refunds; I found two in the other drawer.” That's reporting an access failure with its context. Rule: “couldn't check” must never look like “checked, found nothing.”
options: Correct. Say the check failed, what you tried, and what you did find.
Trying the locked cabinet a few more times doesn't help when it stays locked for an hour.
Saying “try again later” is better than “empty”, but leaves out what you already found.
Sending every “empty” folder to a person catches repeats, but buries them in real first-timers.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the answer is to retry harder. But the bug is in the report: a timeout comes back looking like a real empty result, so the coordinator trusts it. The subagent must say the lookup failed, and pass on what it tried and found.
deep.diagram:
timeout → "no refunds"      → coordinator approves (wrong)
timeout → failed + query + partial → hold, escalate or retry
deep.mapTitle: How should a subagent report a lookup?

evidence.quote: When that API times out, the subagent tells the coordinator “No previous refunds found.”
evidence.means: The decider: a failure reported as an empty result. Escalating every empty result ([[3]]) works around this without fixing it.

evidence.quote: The coordinator then approves refunds that repeat earlier ones
evidence.means: The coordinator trusted a result that wasn't real. It needs to know the check failed.

evidence.quote: The API's outages usually last about an hour
evidence.means: Local retries ([[1]]) won't outlast the outage, so the report itself must change.

evidence.quote: How should the subagent report this case?
evidence.means: A failure with the query and partial results, not a bare transient flag ([[2]]): [[0]].

deep.rule: Never report “couldn't check” as “found nothing.” Report the failure with what was tried and any partial results.

guide.quote: Distinguish access failures (retry) from valid empty results.

questions.question: Some refund disputes go on for a long time. When a chat gets close to the context limit, the SDK replaces older turns with a summary. After that, the agent sometimes offers a smaller refund than it promised earlier. It also forgets which items the customer said were missing. Which change best fixes this?

options.t: Before each refund offer, have the agent call lookup_order again to reload the order and its items.
options.why: Works, but only for what the order system knows. It reloads the order, but the promised amount and the items the customer reported missing were said in the chat, not stored there.

options.t: Raise the threshold for summarising older turns, so more of each chat stays word for word.
options.why: Works, but only delays it. More of each chat stays word for word, but long disputes still cross the threshold and the same facts get blurred.

options.t: Tell the summariser to quote every amount and item mentioned in the earlier turns.
options.why: Works, but still lossy. A careful summary keeps most amounts, but the facts go through a summary on every pass, and each pass can drop or change them.

options.t: Keep a case-facts block of promised amounts, missing items and order IDs in every request.
options.why: Best. Facts kept outside the summarised history survive every summary, and the agent sees them on every turn.

questions.decider: After that, the agent sometimes offers a smaller refund than it promised earlier.
questions.explanation: Summarising blurs numbers, dates and promises. Pull them into a persistent case-facts block that is sent with every request instead of being summarised.

eli5.question: To save space, old parts of the chat get squeezed into a summary. After that, the agent forgets what it promised. The clue: the facts get lost in the summary.
eli5.answer: When a long meeting is summarised, exact numbers get rounded off. A good assistant keeps a separate card with the key facts: “promised $40 credit; salmon and rice missing”. The summary can be rough; the card stays exact. That card is a case-facts block sent with every request. Rule: numbers and promises that must survive go in a facts block, not the summary.
options: Re-reading the order helps, but the promises were made in the chat, not in the order.
Summarising later only moves the problem further down the chat.
A better summary is still a summary; numbers can still slip.
Correct. Keep the key facts on a separate card that never gets summarised.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a better summary will keep the facts. But every summary is a lossy step, and a long chat gets summarised again and again. Exact facts such as amounts, items and promises should not depend on a summary at all. Keep them in a separate block that goes with every request.
deep.diagram:
older turns   → summary (blurry)     ┐
case facts: $40 credit, salmon      ├→ every request
recent turns  (word for word)       ┘
deep.mapTitle: Facts go missing in a long session. Where are they lost?

Cause

evidence.quote: When a chat gets close to the context limit, the SDK replaces older turns with a summary
evidence.means: Facts from early turns now exist only inside summaries.

evidence.quote: After that, the agent sometimes offers a smaller refund than it promised earlier
evidence.means: The decider. The loss starts after summarising, so the summary is the cause. Reloading the order ([[0]]) doesn't bring back what was promised in the chat.

evidence.quote: It also forgets which items the customer said were missing
evidence.means: More than one kind of fact is lost, so a better summary prompt ([[2]]) or a later threshold ([[1]]) only reduces or delays it.

evidence.quote: Which change best fixes this?
evidence.means: Take the facts out of the summarised history: [[3]].

deep.rule: Exact facts that must survive a long chat go into a case-facts block, not into summaries.

guide.obj: 5.1 Preserve critical information across long interactions
guide.quote: Extract transactional facts into a persistent "case facts" block
